summary: Offers guidelines for authors of SIP extensions. SIP is easy to extend, and this document advises on how to do it so that extensions stay effective and interoperable. It is informational.

eli5.summary: SIP is like building blocks that you can add to. This is a how-to for adding new blocks so they fit with the rest.

subtitle: Best practices for extending the Session Initiation Protocol with new features.

tldr.problem: SIP is designed to be extensible with new methods, header fields, and body types, but extensions can easily break interoperability, violate SIP's architecture, or create operational complexity if not designed carefully.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC provides guidelines to help extension authors: first, decide whether the problem is appropriate for SIP; second, understand SIP's solution space and architectural assumptions; and third, address backward compatibility, security, and syntactic issues.
tldr.outcome: Authors who follow these guidelines can extend SIP while maintaining backward compatibility with existing implementations and preserving the simplicity and generality that makes SIP successful.

today: RFC 4485 is an Informational RFC and remains the primary guide for SIP extension authors. It has not been obsoleted, and the principles it outlines continue to be foundational for maintaining SIP's simplicity and interoperability as the protocol is extended.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) is a simple and flexible protocol for initiating, modifying, and terminating interactive communications sessions. Part of that flexibility comes from the ease with which it can be extended with new methods (like INVITE or CANCEL), new header fields, new body types, and new parameters.

However, extensions are not created equal. Some extensions break backward compatibility with existing implementations. Others violate fundamental SIP architectural assumptions, making the protocol less coherent. Still others introduce operational complexity through cascading requirements on multiple devices.

This RFC provides technical guidelines to help extension authors navigate these pitfalls, ensuring that extensions are appropriate, well-designed, and interoperable.
sections.eli5: SIP is a building-block protocol that you can add to. This is a how-to for adding blocks so everything still works together.

sections.title: Is a SIP Extension Appropriate?
sections.content:
The first question when designing an extension is whether SIP is the right place for the feature at all. SIP's core purpose is session initiation: discovering users wherever they may be, delivering session descriptions, and routing responses. Personal mobility, automatic call distribution, and follow-me services are natural extensions.

However, many problems are outside SIP's solution space. SIP is not a session management protocol (the session's content and behavior are outside SIP). It is not a resource reservation protocol, not a general-purpose transfer protocol, not a configuration protocol, and not a device control protocol. Some features found in traditional phone networks are not appropriate for SIP's distributed, Internet-scale architecture.

A good test: if the extension solves a narrow problem specific to one vendor's implementation or one use case, rather than a generic problem applicable to many session types, it probably doesn't belong in SIP. Similarly, if SIP messages must carry large amounts of data unrelated to session setup, HTTP or another protocol is more appropriate.
sections.eli5: Just because you can add something to SIP does not mean you should. Ask whether SIP's job (finding people and setting up calls) is really the right place for this feature.

sections.title: Core Architectural Principles
sections.content:
SIP is built on several fundamental architectural assumptions that extensions must respect. Session independence means SIP operation does not depend on the type of session (audio, video, chat, or game). An extension that only works for audio violates this.

Path independence means SIP messages and session packets travel completely different paths through the network. Extensions must not assume they are coupled. Multi-provider operation means SIP works across multiple networks and many hops; extensions must not require a single provider or single hop.

Transactional operation means SIP is request/response at heart. Proxy scalability means proxies must be able to forward messages with minimal processing; they often ignore message bodies and do not need to understand all methods. Full state in INVITE means an initial INVITE is nearly identical to a re-INVITE, so no state should need to span multiple INVITEs.

Extensions that violate these assumptions may work in controlled environments but break in the broader Internet. A new method that proxies must understand, or an extension that only works when signaling and media paths are coupled, are examples of violations.
sections.eli5: SIP is built to work anywhere, for any kind of call, across many hops and providers. Extensions that assume a simpler world will break eventually.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility and Interoperability
sections.content:
The most critical issue for extensions is backward compatibility. If an extension adds header fields or parameters that existing implementations must understand to process a request, the extension must use the Require or Proxy-Require header fields to signal that the extension is required. Without these headers, old implementations will silently ignore the extension and potentially behave incorrectly.

However, using Require creates an interoperability problem: if any entity in the path does not understand the extension, the request fails with a 420 (Bad Extension) response. The sender can retry without the extension, but as the number of possible extensions grows, this leads to an exponential explosion of combinations.

For this reason, Proxy-Require is strongly discouraged. Each proxy in the path increases failure likelihood, and with many hops, failure becomes nearly certain. Require is bad enough for basic session services (session initiation and termination), but at least it only requires understanding by the final recipient.

New methods avoid Require altogether: SIP already has mechanisms (OPTIONS, Allow header) for discovering which methods a server understands. For new header fields, the Supported header field mechanism allows a server to discover what a client can handle. Extensions should leverage these mechanisms rather than mandate support with Require.
sections.eli5: When you add to SIP, old phones should not break. If they must understand a new feature, use Require carefully. Better yet, design the extension so old implementations can ignore it safely.

sections.title: Technical Guidelines for Extensions
sections.content:
New method names should use all capital letters, be shorter than 10 characters, and convey the general meaning (e.g., REFER for transfer, PRACK for provisional acknowledgment). Header fields should have descriptive names with each word capitalized (e.g., Session-Timer) and should be brief unless they are heavily used.

All extensions must consider security. Extensions should not require new security capabilities beyond what SIP already provides. If an extension introduces new authorization requirements or needs end-to-end integrity, document these clearly. Be careful not to conflate SIP signaling security with media session security; they use different mechanisms.

Every extension must address terminology consistently with RFC 3261 and avoid defining new terms for concepts already named in other SIP specifications. Syntax must be defined precisely using ABNF, making clear what is case-sensitive and what is not.

Most importantly, extensions must define clear semantics: what the extension does, when it applies, how it interacts with existing features, and what happens when different implementations support different versions of the extension.
sections.eli5: When designing the technical details, use clear names, think about security, be consistent with existing SIP terminology, and document exactly what your extension does and doesn't do.

sections.title: Specifics for Methods, Headers, and Body Types
sections.content:
Extensions that define new methods do not need Require: proxies can forward new methods without understanding them because SIP is method-agnostic. The exception is if a new method must be understood by proxies (to be processed correctly), which makes the extension problematic and should be avoided.

For new header fields added by proxies or servers, the Supported header mechanism is recommended. A server checks whether the client's request includes the extension in the Supported header field before adding the header field to a response. This preserves backward compatibility: if the client does not support the extension, the header field is not sent.

New body types (like a new media description format) are trickier because bodies must be understood to process messages correctly. The Content-Disposition header field can mark bodies as optional for processing. For messages that establish dialogs, both parties should exchange Accept header fields to indicate which body types they support, allowing both to determine what body types are safe to send.

If a body must be understood, it is best if the sender knows the recipient supports it before sending. Include Accept in requests and responses to negotiate supported body types, avoiding situations where a receiver gets a body type it cannot process.
sections.eli5: If you are adding a new command, old routers can usually forward it without changes. If you are adding information to a response, ask the client first if it can understand it. If you are adding data, mark it optional or negotiate support before using it.
